document.title: Enterprise Spring Microservices Template Architecture
document.subtitle: C4 views of the Enterprise Spring Microservices Template for **architects and new engineers**: context, containers, components and six runtime flows. Written by hand from the repository at its current commit; no Lantern output.

revisions.author: Independent second pass
revisions.summary: Verified against the code: sign-in redirects reach the BFF directly, realm import only on an empty database, role checks narrowed, browser edges are HTTP; two risks added.

web-user.name: Web user
web-user.description: Signs in through the web app, keeps one personal profile, and creates and lists their own orders.

properties.access: Any Keycloak user of realm my-realm; no role checks on profile or order endpoints

mobile-app.name: Mobile app
mobile-app.description: The "mobile lane": a native app that signs in at Keycloak with PKCE (mobile-client) and calls the API gateway with bearer tokens. Not in this repository.

angular-ui.name: angular-ui
angular-ui.description: Browser UI for sign-in, registration and confirmation, profile and orders; sends every call to /bff with cookies and X-Requested-With, and never sees a token.

properties.stack: Angular ^22.1.7, Angular Material, RxJS 7.8, TypeScript ~6.0; built on node:24-alpine, served by nginx:alpine, which proxies /bff/ to the BFF

bff.name: bff
bff.description: OAuth2 client for the web app: runs the Keycloak login, keeps the tokens in Redis behind a signed BFF_SESSION cookie, refreshes them early and proxies /bff/api and /bff/public calls to the gateway.

gateway.name: gateway
gateway.technology: Spring Cloud Gateway Server WebFlux · Boot 4.1.1 / Java 25
gateway.description: Single API entry for the BFF and the mobile app: validates the JWT and its audience, rate-limits with Redis, applies circuit breakers and routes /profile, /orders and /admin to the services.

properties.stack: Spring Cloud 2025.1.3, OAuth2 resource server, reactive Redis, Resilience4j, springdoc webflux

profile.name: profile-service
profile.description: User profiles, self-registration with email confirmation, and the administrator's create and delete user saga; asks keycloak-admin-service to create Keycloak users.

properties.stack: Spring Data JPA, Flyway, OAuth2 resource server and client (client credentials), RestClient, springdoc, common-security

order.name: order-service
order.description: Creates orders and lists the caller's own orders; the owner is the JWT subject, recorded by JPA auditing.

properties.stack: Spring Data JPA with auditing, Flyway, OAuth2 resource server, springdoc, common-security

kc-admin.name: keycloak-admin-service
kc-admin.description: Thin proxy to the Keycloak Admin API: creates and deletes users for administrators and creates self-registered users for profile-service.

properties.stack: keycloak-admin-client 26.0.12, OAuth2 resource server, common-security; no database

keycloak.name: Keycloak
keycloak.description: Off-the-shelf identity provider run by this repository with its own realm export (my-realm): logs users in, issues 5-minute access tokens with rotating refresh tokens, holds users and roles.

properties.stack: quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.7.4, realm imported from keycloak/realm-config at startup (Keycloak skips it once the realm exists in its database)

redis.name: Redis
redis.description: BFF sessions (bff:session:<jti>, 30 min TTL), refresh locks, the Spring Session behind JSESSIONID, and the gateway's rate-limit buckets.

profile-db.name: profile_db
profile-db.description: user_profiles and pending_registrations (confirmation token, expiry). Schema by Flyway.

order-db.name: order_db
order-db.description: orders with globally unique order numbers, status, audit columns and an optimistic-lock version. Schema by Flyway.

keycloak-db.name: keycloak (database)
keycloak-db.description: Keycloak's own store: realm, clients, users, credentials and sessions.

bff-login.name: Login and identity
bff-login.description: Starts the Keycloak login, and on success stores the tokens as a BffSession under a new jti and sets the BFF_SESSION cookie; /bff/user returns the OIDC user from the JSESSIONID session.

bff-guard.name: Security chain
bff-guard.description: CSRF with a readable XSRF-TOKEN cookie, CORS for the web origin, strict security headers, and 401 instead of a redirect for AJAX calls.

bff-refresh.name: Proactive token refresh
bff-refresh.description: Before a /bff/api call, refreshes an access token that expires within 60 s under a per-session Redis lock; deletes the session when Keycloak rejects the refresh token.

bff-proxy.name: API proxy
bff-proxy.description: Forwards /bff/api/** with the session's bearer token and /bff/public/{service}/** without one to the gateway, behind one circuit breaker (503 when open, 502 when unreachable).

bff-logout.name: Single sign-out
bff-logout.description: Deletes the Redis session, invalidates JSESSIONID, clears both cookies and redirects to Keycloak's end-session endpoint with the ID token.

bff-session-jwt.name: Session cookie signer
bff-session-jwt.description: Signs and verifies the BFF_SESSION JWT (jti, 30-minute expiry); uses an ephemeral key outside prod when no key is set.

bff-session-store.name: Session store
bff-session-store.description: Saves, loads and deletes BffSession records under bff:session:<jti> with a 30-minute TTL.

gw-security.name: JWT check
gw-security.description: Rejects any request without a valid Keycloak JWT carrying audience template-api, except /*/public/**, health, Swagger and /fallback; no role checks.

gw-routes.name: Route table
gw-routes.description: Maps /profile/**, /orders/** and /admin/** to the services, stripping the first segment and adding /api; answers 403 on /admin/users/register.

gw-ratelimit.name: Rate limiter
gw-ratelimit.description: Token bucket of 10 requests/s, burst 20, keyed by user, or by the caller's address when anonymous.

gw-breaker.name: Circuit breakers
gw-breaker.description: One breaker per route with a 5 s time limit; forwards to /fallback, which answers 503 Problem Details.

ps-security.name: JWT check
ps-security.description: Validates the JWT and audience, maps realm roles to ROLE_*, permits /api/public/** and enables @PreAuthorize.

ps-profile-api.name: Profile API
ps-profile-api.description: Gets, creates and deletes the caller's own profile, keyed by the JWT subject.

ps-registration.name: Registration
ps-registration.description: Public register (same 201 for every email) and confirm; creates a disabled profile and pending registration, and on confirmation the Keycloak user.

ps-admin-api.name: Admin user API
ps-admin-api.description: Creates a Keycloak user and then its profile (deleting the user if that fails), or deletes the profile and then the Keycloak user.

ps-email.name: Confirmation email
ps-email.description: Only implementation logs the confirmation link (not under prod); no email is actually sent.

ps-kc-client.name: Keycloak admin client
ps-kc-client.description: Calls keycloak-admin-service with the caller's token for admin calls, or with an internal-client token for registration.

ps-repos.name: Repositories
ps-repos.description: Read and write user profiles and pending registrations.

os-security.name: JWT check
os-security.description: Validates the JWT and audience; every order endpoint needs a signed-in user.

os-orders-api.name: Orders API
os-orders-api.description: Creates an order with status CREATED and pages the caller's orders.

os-auditing.name: Auditor
os-auditing.description: Fills createdBy and updatedBy from the JWT subject and the timestamps.

os-repo.name: Order repository
os-repo.description: Stores orders and finds them by createdBy.

ka-security.name: JWT and role check
ka-security.description: Validates the JWT and audience; user creation and deletion need ADMIN, registration needs INTERNAL_SERVICE.

ka-api.name: User admin API
ka-api.description: Creates users (with a password, or without one plus an UPDATE_PASSWORD email) and deletes them.

ka-client.name: Keycloak Admin client
ka-client.description: Talks to the Keycloak Admin REST API as the admin-service-client service account (manage-users, view-users).

pages.title: Enterprise Spring Microservices Template
pages.summary: A template for secured Spring microservices: users sign in with Keycloak, keep a profile and place orders, from a web app through a Backend for Frontend or from a mobile app directly against the API gateway. The most important fact for anyone changing it: **the browser never holds a token**; the BFF keeps them in Redis, and every hop behind it validates the JWT again.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
This document is for **architects and new engineers**. It was written by hand from the code of the one repository at the commit listed under Sources (2026-09-21), on 2026-10-29. Lantern produced none of it.

The repository explains several choices in `docs/` and the README but records no owners or quality goals; where this document needs one it says *unknown*. People and external systems below are only those the code shows.

items.label: Runtime units
items.note: 1 web app, 1 BFF, 1 gateway, 3 services, Keycloak

items.label: User roles
items.note: ADMIN and plain users; INTERNAL_SERVICE for service calls

items.label: External systems
items.note: A mobile app, outside this repository

sections.body: Left out on purpose: Zipkin, Prometheus, Loki and Grafana only receive traces, metrics and logs, and GitLab CI only builds. None takes part in a user request. No email provider appears: confirmation links are only logged, and Keycloak has no SMTP server configured. Keycloak is drawn as a container because this repository runs it with its own realm configuration.

pages.title: Requests and data
pages.summary: How a request reaches the services: the web app through nginx and the BFF, the mobile app and API clients straight to the gateway, and which store each container owns.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
The web app's calls go to its own origin: nginx (or the Angular dev server) proxies `/bff/` to the **BFF**; only the sign-in redirects take the browser straight to the BFF's published port 8081 (the realm's redirect URI) and to Keycloak. The BFF adds the user's bearer token and calls the **gateway**. The gateway validates the token, rate-limits through Redis and routes `/profile`, `/orders` and `/admin` to the three services, rewriting the prefix to `/api`. Each service validates the token again. profile-service calls keycloak-admin-service directly, not through the gateway.

**common-core, common-web and common-security** are not containers: they are libraries compiled into the services (error handling, trailing-slash handling, the resource-server security chain).

sections.title: Deployments
rows: Infrastructure only: Redis 8, three PostgreSQL 18 (keycloak, profile_db, order_db), Keycloak 26.7.4, Zipkin, Prometheus, Loki, Grafana.
The Java services and the Angular dev server then run on the host, via `manage_services.sh start` and `npm start`.
Adds the five Java services, built from the shared `Dockerfile`, and angular-ui (nginx) on `sec-network`.
The browser must resolve `keycloak` to 127.0.0.1; every container also publishes its port on the host.
Builds and tests, scans with Trivy, and on the default branch or tags builds the images.
No registry push and no deployment job; no Kubernetes or other production descriptor exists.

pages.title: Identity and tokens
pages.summary: Who talks to Keycloak and why: the BFF runs the login and refreshes tokens, every resource server checks signatures against Keycloak's keys, and two services hold their own service accounts.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Access tokens live **5 minutes** and refresh tokens rotate (single use). The BFF uses the confidential `bff-client`; the mobile app the public `mobile-client` with PKCE; profile-service gets client-credentials tokens as `internal-client` (role INTERNAL_SERVICE) to call the registration endpoint; keycloak-admin-service uses `admin-service-client` with realm-management rights. All user-facing clients add the audience `template-api` that every resource server requires.

items: Two sessions: JSESSIONID (Spring Session in Redis) for `/bff/user`, BFF_SESSION for `/bff/api/**`.

Only Authorization, Content-Type, Accept and Accept-Language are forwarded to the gateway.

sections.title: No decision records
sections.body: The repository has no architecture decision records, but its `docs/` folder and README explain several choices. Decisions below cite that rationale where it exists and say *not recorded* otherwise.

items.title: Decoupled BFF service for the web app
items.body: A separate Spring MVC BFF runs the OAuth2 login and proxies to the gateway, instead of a BFF inside the gateway. Rationale recorded: single responsibility, room to aggregate, three verification layers (`docs/bff_comparison_analysis.md:33-39`).

items.title: Two client lanes
items.body: Web: cookie session through the BFF. Mobile: OIDC with PKCE and bearer tokens straight to the gateway (`README.md:24-25`; `docs/bff_comparison_analysis.md:41-47`).

items.title: Defense in depth: every hop validates the JWT
items.body: The gateway and each service validate signature, issuer and audience `template-api`; profile-service's admin endpoints and keycloak-admin-service also check realm roles (the gateway and order-service check none). Rationale recorded: no trusted internal network (`docs/defense_in_depth_vs_perimeter.md:31-37`; `README.md:348-355`).

items.title: Tokens never reach the browser
items.body: The BFF keeps access, refresh and ID tokens in Redis as JSON (no client secret, no Java serialization) behind a signed BFF_SESSION cookie (`BffSession.java:9-31`; `RedisConfig.java:11-20`).

items.title: Two BFF sessions
items.body: JSESSIONID (Spring Session in Redis) for /bff/user and the login; BFF_SESSION for the proxy, so refresh is under the BFF's control (`README.md:459-464`; `docs/dual_session_strategy.md:83-97`).

items.title: Proactive, race-safe token refresh
items.body: Refresh 60 s before expiry, one refresher per session through a Redis lock, because the realm rotates refresh tokens (`README.md:407-433`; `docs/proactive_token_refresh.md:39-65`).

items.title: Keycloak user only after email confirmation, no password collected
items.body: Unconfirmed registrations live only in profile_db; the password is set through Keycloak's own email; every registration answer is the same 201 (`docs/user_registration_flow.md:69-117`).

items.title: User administration through a dedicated service
items.body: keycloak-admin-service alone holds the realm-management service account; profile-service calls it (`README.md:278`; `KeycloakConfig.java:25-33`). Rationale: not recorded.

items.title: Database per service, schema by Flyway
items.body: profile_db and order_db on separate PostgreSQL instances, Hibernate only validates (`README.md:665-671`). Rationale: not recorded.

items.title: Reactive gateway for the Redis rate limiter
items.body: Rationale recorded: Spring Cloud Gateway WebFlux was chosen for its Redis RequestRateLimiter (`README.md:292`).

items.title: Shared libraries and one Dockerfile
items.body: common-web and common-security auto-configure error handling and the resource-server chain; one multi-stage Dockerfile builds every Java service (`README.md:223-265`; `Dockerfile:1-14`).

sections.title: Risks and findings
rows: Default credentials are live: the realm export, imported when Keycloak first starts on an empty database, holds the client secrets and users `admin`/`password` (ADMIN) and `user`/`password`; `test-client` allows the password grant and adds audience `template-api`. Keycloak runs `start-dev`, and its bootstrap console admin defaults to `admin`/`admin`.

Unless every default is overridden, anyone who reaches Keycloak can get an ADMIN token that all services accept, and create or delete users, or take over the whole Keycloak server through the admin console.
Self-registered users probably cannot set a password: the realm configures no SMTP server, and keycloak-admin-service logs and ignores the failed UPDATE_PASSWORD email and still answers 201.
Registration "succeeds" but the new Keycloak user has no password and no way to get the email again.
No email sender exists for confirmation links: the only EmailService logs the link and is disabled under `prod`.
In production profile-service does not start until one is written; elsewhere confirmation links are only in the logs.
An unconfirmed or expired registration blocks its email for good: register silently does nothing when any profile has the email, and no cleanup job exists.
A visitor whose link expired cannot register again with the same address.
Confirmation is not atomic across Keycloak and profile_db: the Keycloak user is created inside the database transaction.
If the save or commit fails, the Keycloak user stays and every retry of the link fails with 500 because the username exists.
Anonymous web traffic shares one rate-limit bucket: public calls reach the gateway from the BFF without a token or X-Forwarded-For, and TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS is 0.
All visitors together get 10 requests/s for registration and confirmation; one noisy client blocks everyone.
Single instances: one Redis holds BFF sessions, Spring sessions, refresh locks and rate-limit state; one Keycloak in dev mode with one PostgreSQL; no HA in the repository.
Losing Redis logs every web user out and fails gateway readiness; losing Keycloak stops all sign-ins and token refreshes.
BFF_SESSION expires 30 minutes after login whatever the activity: it is issued only at login, and refresh renews only the Redis record.
Active web users are sent back through the Keycloak login every 30 minutes.
Order numbers are made in the browser (`ORD-` + random below 10000) but must be unique across all users.
Collisions give 409 once there are a few hundred orders.
The profile `enabled` flag is inconsistent and unused: admin-created profiles stay false, self-registered ones become true.
Business logic cannot rely on it as the docs suggest.
Confirmation tokens are stored in plain text, while admin-service Javadoc says a BCrypt hash is stored; confirmation is a state-changing GET.
A database reader can confirm pending registrations; link scanners can confirm by fetching the link.
Every container publishes its port on the host, including PostgreSQL, Redis and the services.
Direct calls bypass the gateway's rate limiting and circuit breakers (the JWT is still checked).

A profile's email is whatever the client sends: `POST /api` takes the email from the request body and never compares it with the token, while `user_profiles.email` is unique and registration silently skips any email already in it.
Any signed-in user can claim someone else's address in their profile, and that person can then never self-register with it.

No transport security by default: every hop is plain HTTP (nginx on 4200, Keycloak with `KC_HTTP_ENABLED`, the services), the BFF_SESSION cookie is not `Secure` unless `BFF_COOKIE_SECURE` is set, and Redis runs without TLS.
Outside a trusted network, session cookies and bearer tokens travel in clear text; production needs TLS added in front of or inside every container.

Stale or missing documentation: the README diagram puts the order database on 5433 (it is 5434); the admin profile endpoints sit at `/profile/profile/admin/users` through the gateway, which no document mentions; and `.env.example` says its values work out of the box, but its `changeme` client secrets do not match the realm export.
New engineers are misled about ports and paths; a copied `.env.example` breaks sign-in and service calls until the realm's secrets are changed to match.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How the system runs in production: only Docker Compose exists, and CI builds images without pushing them anywhere.
The mobile app: the README and the realm (`mobile-client`) describe it, but no code exists.
Which email provider is meant for confirmation links and for Keycloak's password email.
Owners and quality goals: not recorded.
The order lifecycle: six statuses exist, but no endpoint or job changes an order's status.

sections.title: Glossary
rows: Backend for Frontend: a server that runs the login for the web app and keeps its tokens, so the browser only holds a cookie.
The BFF's own cookie: an RS256-signed JWT whose jti names the Redis record that holds the user's tokens.

The repository's name for the BFF's servlet session cookie, kept in Redis by Spring Session; used only by /bff/user and the login itself. With Spring Session and no cookie name configured, the cookie is most likely named `SESSION` on the wire.
Token claim naming who the token is for; every resource server here requires `template-api`.
OAuth2 grant in which a service gets a token for itself, with no user.
Cross-site request forgery; the BFF requires the XSRF-TOKEN cookie value back on state-changing requests.
The JSON Web Key Set Keycloak publishes; resource servers fetch it to check token signatures.
OpenID Connect, the sign-in protocol on top of OAuth2.
Proof Key for Code Exchange, which protects the authorization-code flow of public clients such as the mobile app.
Keycloak's tenant: here `my-realm`, with its clients, roles and users.
Each refresh token can be used once; the BFF serializes refreshes with a Redis lock because of it.
RFC 9457 error format returned by every service.
